ad9_credit_and_scores.topic: Household debt, card rates, the end of usury caps, credit scores

claims.text: Credit card interest rate, accounts assessed interest (G.19): Nov 2013 12.89%, Nov 2019 16.88%, Nov 2023 22.75%, Nov 2024 22.80%, Nov 2025 22.30%, Aug 2026 22.36%.
Household debt service ratio (TDSP): peak 15.85% Q4 2007; low 9.05% Q1 2021; 11.11% Q2 2026 (series in current vintage begins 2005).

NY Fed Q4 2025: total household debt $18.776tn (+$740bn y/y); credit cards $1.277tn (+$66bn y/y); card flow into 90+ delinquency 7.13%; 4.8% of debt delinquent. Implied Q4 2024: total $18.04tn, cards $1.211tn.
NY Fed Q4 2022: total $16.90tn; cards $986bn (series high, above pre-pandemic high of $927bn); implied Q4 2021 total $15.58tn and cards $856bn.
NY Fed Q4 2019: total $14.15tn, cards $0.93tn; previous peak $12.68tn in Q3 2008.
NY Fed Q4 2016: total $12.58tn, cards $779bn. Q3 2013: total $11.28tn, cards $672bn. Q4 2011: total $11.53tn (as first published).
Q4 2023 total household debt about $17.5tn and card balances about $1.13tn.

Marquette (18 Dec 1978), unanimous, Brennan J.: a national bank may charge out-of-state cardholders the rate allowed in its home state (Nebraska 18% on first $999.99 vs Minnesota 12% cap); protecting state usury laws is for Congress.

Smiley v. Citibank (3 Jun 1996), Scalia J.: deferred to OCC regulation 12 CFR 7.4001(a) (adopted 9 Feb 1996) treating late fees as 'interest' exportable under section 85; the regulation lists late fees, NSF fees, overlimit, annual, cash advance and membership fees.

Janklow: South Dakota law passed in one day with an emergency clause; Citibank helped draft it; Citibank came in 1981; promised 400 jobs, later about 3,000 employees; he said he helped foster consumer-credit effects.

Colorado opted out of state-bank rate exportation (DIDMCA s.525) in 2023; district court preliminary injunction; 2-1 Tenth Circuit panel upheld opt-out 10 Nov 2025; en banc rehearing granted 2 Apr 2026, panel decision vacated (National Ass'n of Industrial Bankers v. Weiser).
CARD Act (effective 22 Feb 2010) statements must show payoff time and total cost at minimum payments and the monthly payment to pay off in 36 months.
CFPB (22 Feb 2024): average card APR rose from 12.9% (2013) to 22.8% (2023); APR margin over prime at all-time high (about 14.3 points in 2023); CFPB attributed it to issuers raising margins.

Consumer Bankers Association rebuttal (29 Feb 2024): CFPB large-vs-small comparison skewed by credit unions' 18% cap; gap 2.2-5 points; large issuers serve more subprime customers, offer more rewards.
FICO created its general-purpose credit score in 1989; all three bureaus used FICO scores by 1991.

FICO score weights: payment history 35%, amounts owed 30%, length of history 15%, new credit 10%, credit mix 10%; does not consider race, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, age, income, employment.

FTC Section 319 study (Dec 2012): 1,001 consumers; 26% found at least one potentially material error; 13% had an error that changed their score; 5% had errors that lowered their score enough to likely raise the cost of credit.
CFPB (23 Jun 2025): corrected credit-invisible share for 2010 from 11.0% (25.9m) to 5.8% (13.5m); 2.7% (about 7.0m adults) in 2020; unscored records 9.8% of adults in 2020.

Fed 2007 report: scoring cut mortgage decision times from weeks to minutes and costs up to 50%; consistency may reduce discrimination; but very little evidence that expansion disproportionately benefited historically underserved groups (tentative).

FHFA 22 Apr 2026 announced limited initial VantageScore 4.0 use at the GSEs; Fannie Mae LL-2026-06 (9 Sep 2026) opened VantageScore 4.0 to all approved lenders, effective immediately, Classic FICO still allowed; tri-merge retained.

CFPB medical-debt credit-report rule vacated by Judge Sean Jordan (E.D. Tex.) in July 2025; it would have removed about $49bn from 15m reports; bureaus' voluntary 2023 changes (paid medical debt removed, under $500 not reported) remain.
FRED TERMCBCCALLNS (audit re-check), November values: 1998 15.67%, 2005 12.58%, 2010 13.44%, 2015 12.22%, 2018 14.73%; Nov 2023 and Nov 2024 both 21.47%.

ad9_fees_and_unbanked.topic: Overdraft and late fees, the unbanked, check cashing and prepaid

claims.text: Public Law 119-10, approved 9 May 2025, disapproved the CFPB overdraft rule published 30 Dec 2024 (89 FR 106768).
S.J.Res.18 passed Senate 52-48 (27 Mar 2025) and House 217-211 (9 Apr 2025); rule covered institutions over $10bn; options: $5 fee, breakeven fee, or TILA credit terms.

CFPB final overdraft rule (Dec 2024): banks and credit unions over $10bn; $5 or breakeven; up to $5bn a year savings, $225 per overdraft-paying household; effective 1 Oct 2025; the Fed exempted overdraft from TILA in 1969.
ABA (Rob Nichols, 5 Mar 2025): rule 'flawed and unlawful from the start'; most Americans value overdraft coverage; price limits would make the service harder to offer.
CFPB March 2024 late-fee rule set an $8 safe harbor (previously up to $30 first/$41 later); NCLC estimated $10bn a year; CFPB joined industry in a consent motion to vacate (filed 14 Apr 2025).
Judge Mark Pittman (N.D. Tex.) vacated the late-fee rule 15 Apr 2025; the rule cut the safe harbor from $32 to $8; CFPB agreed it violated the CARD Act's 'reasonable and proportional' standard.

FDIC 2023: 4.2% of households (5.6m) unbanked (8.2% in 2011); 14.2% (19.0m) underbanked; main reason: not enough money for minimum balance (23.3%), distrust 15.7%; fee/minimum reasons 33.4%; Black 10.6%, Hispanic 9.5%, AIAN 12.2%; working-age disabled 11.2% vs 3.7%; 21.6% of unbanked used prepaid cards; 66.2% cash only; 78.4% of unbanked had no mainstream credit; two-thirds of decline since 2011 linked to socioeconomic change.
New York caps check-cashing fees at 1.5% for government benefit checks and the greater of $1 or 2.2% for other checks (effective 18 Jan 2023).
CFPB prepaid rule took effect 1 Apr 2019: short-form fee chart on package, error and fraud protection after registration, limits on overdraft features.

SHED 2025: 63% of adults would cover a $400 expense with cash or equivalent (68% in 2021); 94% of adults had a bank account (77% under $25,000 income); 16% used BNPL in 2025; 11% of BNPL users had a BNPL payment trigger an overdraft or NSF fee.

CFPB funding: on 25 Sep 2026 the D. Or. (State of New York v. Vought) held the acting director unlawfully requested $0 from the Fed; related cases on appeal; House committee advanced a bill to move CFPB to appropriations.

NCLC (3 Jun 2026): top-20 bank overdraft revenue about $4bn in 2025, up 6.2% from 2023; about a quarter of people live in households that pay overdraft fees each year; BMO raised its overdraft fee from $15 to $20 in 2026 and cut its no-fee cushion from $50 to $20.

CFPB (Apr 2024), banks over $1bn: overdraft/NSF revenue $11.96bn (2019), $7.61bn (2022), $5.83bn (2023); about $6.1bn annual reduction vs 2019, about $185 per overdrafting household; 'the vast majority of NSF fees have been eliminated'; earlier CFPB research: nearly 80% of fees paid by under 9% of accountholders (more than 10 overdrafts a year).

FDIC 2023 survey (audit re-check): responses from almost 30,000 households; White unbanked rate 1.9% (Figures ES.2/ES.6); Black-White and Hispanic-White gaps 'were present at every income level'; 10.0% of unbanked households had a traditional credit card vs 79.3% of banked; higher unbanked rates among lower-income, less-educated, Black, Hispanic, AIAN, working-age disabled, highly variable income and single-parent households; about two-thirds of the 2011-2023 decline associated with changes in household circumstances, mainly income and education.

Goodwin (Oct 2026) on State of New York v. Vought, No. 6:25-cv-02384-AA (D. Or., 25 Sep 2026): partial summary judgment for 22 states and DC; acting director unlawfully declined to request FY2026 funding from the Fed (said '$0'); court vacated the decisions but did not enjoin FY2026 funding; NTEU v. Vought on appeal to D.C. Cir., Rise Economy v. Vought to 9th Cir.; House Financial Services advanced the CFPA Accountability and Reform Act of 2026 (appropriations).

ad9_new_lenders.topic: Payday, BNPL, earned-wage access, app lenders, medical credit cards

claims.text: CFPB: $15 per $100 for a two-week payday loan equals an APR of almost 400% ($15/14 days x 365 = about 391%).

CFPB 2014: more than 80% of payday loans rolled over or renewed within 14 days; about half of loans in sequences of 10 or more; 22% of new loans renewed six or more times; one in five monthly-paid borrowers in debt all year.

Pew 2012: 12m borrowers a year spend over $7bn; average eight loans of $375 a year, about $520 in interest, in debt about five months; 69% of first-time borrowers used for recurring expenses, 16% for emergencies; usage 2.9% in strictest states vs 6.6% in least regulated.
CFPB 2017 payday rule (Oct 2017); underwriting provisions rescinded 7 Jul 2020 before taking effect; payment provisions retained; 17 states and DC ban or limit rates (CRS 2020).

Payment provisions (no further withdrawals after two consecutive failed attempts; notices) took effect 30 Mar 2025; CFPB said it would not prioritise enforcement; 2026 regulatory agenda (6 Jul 2026) planned a deregulatory NPRM to reconsider them.
CRL: Rhode Island (signed 9 Jul 2025, effective 1 Jan 2027) became the 21st state plus DC to cap payday rates at 36%; typical RI payday APR 261%.
Military Lending Act (2006) caps the military APR at 36% for covered credit; DoD 2015 rule extended coverage to most consumer credit (compliance 3 Oct 2016; cards 3 Oct 2017).

CFSA (Shaul, 2016): payday loans are demand-driven; often the least expensive option vs bounced checks and late fees; state regulation suffices; CFPB rule would 'effectively end payday lending as it currently exists'.

Morse (JFE 2011): after natural disasters in California, foreclosures rose about 4.5 per 1,000 homes; access to payday lenders offset 1.0-1.3 of them; fewer larcenies; no effect for insured disasters.
CFPB withdrew the 2024 BNPL interpretive rule on 12 May 2025.

CFPB Jan 2025 BNPL report (six lenders): about 277m loans, $34bn GMV in 2022; over 60% of originations in 2021-22 to subprime or deep-subprime borrowers; about 63% had simultaneous loans; BNPL users' card utilisation 60-66% vs 34%; not evidence of causation.

CFPB advisory opinion (23 Dec 2025): payroll-deduction, non-recourse EWA within accrued wages, with no credit underwriting, is not credit under TILA; expedite fees and tips not finance charges; rescinded the July 2024 interpretive rule; California DFPI regulating EWA.

California DFPI 2021 data (as summarised by NCLC): average APR 334% (tip-based) and 331% (non-tip) for EWA/fintech advances; about 36 advances per user per year; most $40-$100; about 10-day term; tips collected 73% of the time; 97% repaid.
FTC v. Brigit (2 Nov 2023): $18m refunds; advertised 'instant' $250 advances few received; $9.99/month subscription hard to cancel; 99-cent 'free' transfer fee.
FTC sued Dave 5 Nov 2024 (misleading advance amounts, undisclosed fees, tips without consent); DOJ amended complaint 30 Dec 2024 adding CEO.
Dave 10-K (2 Mar 2026): motion to dismiss denied 12 Sep 2025; answer filed 10 Oct 2025; no trial date or settlement disclosed; Baltimore sued 30 Dec 2025 (removed to federal court 29 Jan 2026).
Dave called the suit 'government overreach'; eliminated optional tips and express fees for ExtraCash for new members from 4 Dec 2024.

CFPB medical credit cards (May 2023): about $1bn deferred interest 2018-2020; typical APR 26.99% vs about 16% general cards; about one in five promotions not paid off in time; interest assessed averaged about 23% of purchase in 2020; $23bn purchase volume 2018-2020.
CFPB 10 Dec 2013: GE Capital Retail Bank/CareCredit to refund up to $34.1m; enrollment at doctors' and dentists' offices; consumers thought cards interest-free; 26.99% deferred interest.

CFPB's May 2024 interpretive rule classified BNPL providers as credit card issuers under TILA/Regulation Z; on 6 May 2025 the CFPB said it would not prioritise enforcement and would consider rescinding it.

CFPB Jan 2025 BNPL report (audit re-check): consumers averaged just over 100,000 daily applications in 2019 and well over 1 million loans a day by 2022 (six lenders); scaled 277.3m originated loans and $33.8bn GMV in 2022; deep subprime 45.0% and subprime 16.0% of 2021-22 originations.

Pew 2012 (audit re-check): in states with no payday stores, 5 of every 100 would-be borrowers borrow online and 95 do not; 'borrowers are not driven to seek payday loans online or from other sources'; 12m borrowers figure is for 2010; spending 'more than $7 billion' a year.

Sheppard (audit re-check): CFPB announced on 28 Mar 2025, two days before the 30 Mar 2025 compliance date, that it would not prioritise enforcement of the payday payment provisions; Jul 2026 agenda planned an NPRM; no issued NPRM reported on the page.

As of Dave's Q2 2026 report (summarised 5 Aug 2026), the FTC/DOJ suit seeking injunctions and monetary relief was ongoing, with no trial date, settlement or ruling reported; contingency accruals about $10m at 30 Jun 2026, not attributed to this case.
